lesson.title: The Rhythm of AC: Anatomy of a Sinusoidal Waveform
lesson.summary: Alternating current is built from smoothly repeating cosine waves, and every AC signal can be fully described by just three numbers: how big it is, how fast it repeats, and where it starts in its cycle.
lesson.body:
Direct current is simple: voltage and current sit at a constant value. Alternating current is different, and it earns that added complexity for a good reason. Almost every AC source in the real world, from a wall outlet to a power plant generator, comes from a coil of wire spinning inside a magnetic field, and the physics of that rotation produces a voltage that rises and falls exactly like a cosine function. Sinusoids also have a special mathematical property that makes them the natural language of AC circuit analysis: when a sinusoidal voltage is applied to a resistor, inductor, or capacitor, the resulting current is also sinusoidal at the same frequency, only scaled and shifted in time. No other waveform shape survives contact with an inductor or capacitor unchanged.

A general sinusoidal voltage is written as v(t) = Vm cos(ωt + φ). Each symbol carries a distinct piece of information. Vm is the amplitude, the peak value the wave reaches above and below zero. ω is the angular frequency in radians per second, which sets how fast the wave oscillates. φ is the phase angle, which slides the entire wave earlier or later in time without changing its size or speed. These three numbers, amplitude, frequency, and phase angle, completely describe a sinusoid; two sinusoids of the same frequency differ only in amplitude and phase.

Frequency f, measured in hertz, and angular frequency ω are related by ω = 2πf, since one full cycle sweeps through 2π radians. The period T, the time for one complete cycle, is the reciprocal of frequency: T = 1/f = 2π/ω. The argument of the cosine, ωt + φ, must be evaluated in radians, not degrees, even though phase angles are usually quoted in degrees for convenience.

Consider a US wall outlet, often written as v(t) = 170 cos(377t) V. Since ω = 377 rad/s and ω = 2πf, the frequency is f = 377/(2π) = 60.0 Hz, matching the standard US power frequency. The period is T = 1/60 = 0.01667 s, or 16.67 ms. At t = 1/720 s, one twelfth of a period, ωt = 377 × (1/720) = 0.5236 rad = 30°, so v(1/720) = 170 cos(30°) = 170 × 0.8660 = 147.2 V. The 170 V amplitude is the peak value; the familiar "120 volt" rating of a household outlet is instead its rms value, 170/√2 = 120.2 V.

Phase angle becomes essential when comparing two sinusoids of the same frequency, such as a source voltage and the current it drives. If v(t) = 170 cos(377t) V and i(t) = 5 cos(377t − 30°) A, the current reaches its peak 30° after the voltage does. Engineers say the current lags the voltage by 30°, or equivalently the voltage leads the current by 30°. Carrying the shared factor ωt around in every calculation is tedious and unnecessary, since it never changes between two same-frequency signals; the phasor, covered next, strips it away and keeps only the amplitude and phase angle that actually distinguish one sinusoid from another.
